cards.q: Draw the general structure of a 2-amino acid.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{H_{2}NCH(R)COOH}\): an amine group and a carboxylic acid group on the same carbon atom.

answerFigure.alt: Displayed formula of a 2-amino acid: a central carbon bonded to an NH2 group, a hydrogen, an R group and a COOH group (C=O and O–H).

cards.why: It is called a 2-amino acid (α-amino acid) because the NH₂ is on carbon 2, next to the COOH carbon.

cards.q: Is this molecule, 3-aminopropanoic acid, a 2-amino acid?
cards.a: No. It is an amino acid, but the NH₂ is on carbon 3, not on the carbon next to the COOH.
cards.why: The amino acids in proteins all have the NH₂ and COOH on the same carbon.

cards.q: Give the IUPAC name of alanine.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of alanine, 2-aminopropanoic acid: a carbon carrying NH2, CH3 and COOH.

cards.a: 2-aminopropanoic acid
cards.why: Glycine, the simplest amino acid (R = H), is aminoethanoic acid.

cards.q: What is a zwitterion?
cards.a: An ion with both a positive and a negative charge in the same molecule, but no overall charge.
cards.why: In an amino acid the \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) loses \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) to the \(\mathrm{-NH_{2}}\), giving \(\mathrm{-COO^{-}}\) and \(\mathrm{-NH_{3}^{+}}\).

cards.q: Draw the zwitterion of glycine.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of glycine, aminoethanoic acid: NH2–CH2–COOH.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of the zwitterion of glycine: NH3+ at one end and COO− at the other.

cards.why: The proton moves from the acidic COOH group to the basic NH₂ group.

cards.q: Draw the zwitterion of alanine.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of the zwitterion of alanine: a carbon carrying NH3+, CH3 and COO−.

cards.why: Only the NH₂ and COOH groups change; the side chain does not.

cards.q: Draw the ion formed by alanine in strongly acidic solution.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{^{+}H_{3}NCH(CH_{3})COOH}\): a positive ion.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of alanine in acid solution: NH3+ and an un-ionised COOH group.

cards.why: The \(\mathrm{-COO^{-}}\) of the zwitterion accepts \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\), so only the \(\mathrm{-NH_{3}^{+}}\) charge remains.

cards.q: Draw the ion formed by alanine in strongly alkaline solution.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{H_{2}NCH(CH_{3})COO^{-}}\): a negative ion.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of alanine in alkaline solution: an NH2 group and a COO− group.

cards.why: The \(\mathrm{-NH_{3}^{+}}\) of the zwitterion loses \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) to \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\), so only the \(\mathrm{-COO^{-}}\) charge remains.

cards.q: Write equations to show glycine’s zwitterion acting as a base and as an acid.
cards.a:
Base: \(\mathrm{^{+}H_{3}NCH_{2}COO^{-} + H^{+} \rightarrow {}^{+}H_{3}NCH_{2}COOH}\)
Acid: \(\mathrm{^{+}H_{3}NCH_{2}COO^{-} + OH^{-} \rightarrow H_{2}NCH_{2}COO^{-} + H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: Amino acids are amphoteric: they can react with both acids and bases, so they act as buffers.

cards.q: Explain why amino acids are solids with high melting points that dissolve in water.
cards.a: In the solid they exist as zwitterions held by strong ionic attractions.
marks: In the solid, amino acids exist as zwitterions.
There are strong electrostatic attractions between the opposite charges of neighbouring zwitterions.
Much energy is needed to overcome these, so the melting point is high.
The charged groups are strongly attracted to polar water molecules, so they dissolve.

cards.q: True or false: solid glycine is made of \(\mathrm{H_{2}NCH_{2}COOH}\) molecules.
cards.a: False. Solid glycine is made of zwitterions, \(\mathrm{^{+}H_{3}NCH_{2}COO^{-}}\).
cards.why: That is why glycine melts (with decomposition) above 200 °C, unlike a simple molecular compound of similar mass.

cards.q: Why do aqueous solutions of naturally occurring alanine rotate the plane of plane-polarised light?
cards.a: Alanine has a chiral carbon, and living things make only one of its two enantiomers.

answerFigure.alt: The two enantiomers of alanine, drawn with wedge and hashed bonds: mirror images that cannot be superimposed.

cards.why: A single enantiomer rotates plane-polarised monochromatic light; a racemic mixture would not.

cards.q: Which is the only common 2-amino acid that is not optically active, and why?
cards.a: Glycine: its central carbon carries two hydrogen atoms, so it is not chiral.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of glycine, aminoethanoic acid: NH2–CH2–COOH.

cards.why: A chiral carbon needs four different groups. In glycine R = H.

cards.q: What is a peptide link, and how does it form?
cards.a: The amide link \(\mathrm{-CONH-}\) between two amino acids. It forms by condensation: the \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) of one reacts with the \(\mathrm{-NH_{2}}\) of another, eliminating water.
cards.why: Proteins are condensation polymers of amino acids joined by peptide links.

cards.q: Glycine’s COOH group reacts with alanine’s NH₂ group. Draw the dipeptide formed.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{H_{2}NCH_{2}CONHCH(CH_{3})COOH}\) (Gly-Ala) and water.

answerFigure.alt: Displayed formula of the dipeptide Gly-Ala: H2N–CH2–C(=O)–NH–CH(CH3)–COOH, with the peptide link C(=O)–N(H) in the middle.

cards.why: The dipeptide still has a free NH₂ at one end and a free COOH at the other, so the chain can grow.

cards.q: How many different dipeptides can form from one glycine and one alanine molecule? Name them.
cards.a: Two: Gly-Ala and Ala-Gly.

figure.alt: Displayed formula of the dipeptide Gly-Ala: H2N–CH2–C(=O)–NH–CH(CH3)–COOH, with the peptide link C(=O)–N(H) in the middle.

answerFigure.alt: Displayed formula of the dipeptide Ala-Gly: H2N–CH(CH3)–C(=O)–NH–CH2–COOH, with the peptide link C(=O)–N(H) in the middle.

cards.why: Either amino acid can provide the COOH group. The figure with the question is Gly-Ala; with the answer, Ala-Gly.

cards.q: Draw the tripeptide formed from glycine, alanine and serine (\(\mathrm{R = CH_{2}OH}\)), joined in that order.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{H_{2}NCH_{2}CONHCH(CH_{3})CONHCH(CH_{2}OH)COOH}\): two peptide links, two molecules of water eliminated.

answerFigure.alt: Displayed formula of the tripeptide Gly-Ala-Ser: H2N–CH2–CO–NH–CH(CH3)–CO–NH–CH(CH2OH)–COOH, with two peptide links.

cards.why: Write the backbone N–C–C(=O) three times, then add each side chain to its central carbon.

cards.q: Give the conditions for hydrolysing a protein into its amino acids.
cards.a: Heat under reflux with concentrated (about \(6\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\)) hydrochloric acid for several hours.
cards.why: In the acid the amino acids are present as their positive ions, such as \(\mathrm{^{+}H_{3}NCH_{2}COOH}\).

cards.q: This tripeptide is hydrolysed. Name the amino acids formed.

figure.alt: Displayed formula of the tripeptide Gly-Ala-Ser: H2N–CH2–CO–NH–CH(CH3)–CO–NH–CH(CH2OH)–COOH, with two peptide links.

cards.a: Glycine, alanine and serine.
cards.why: Break each \(\mathrm{C(=O){-}NH}\) bond, adding OH to the C and H to the N. The side chains are H, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_{2}OH}\).

cards.q: A peptide is hydrolysed with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide instead of acid. In what form are the amino acids obtained?
cards.a: As their carboxylate ions (sodium salts), for example \(\mathrm{H_{2}NCH_{2}COO^{-}Na^{+}}\).
cards.why: In alkali the COOH group is deprotonated and the NH₂ group stays neutral.

cards.q: How are the amino acids in a protein hydrolysate separated and located by thin-layer chromatography?
cards.a: Spot the mixture on a TLC plate (silica or alumina), develop in a solvent, then spray with ninhydrin and warm, or view under UV light.
cards.why: Ninhydrin turns amino acid spots purple; on a plate with a fluorescent coating, spots show up dark under UV light.

cards.q: On a TLC plate an amino acid spot travels 3.6 cm while the solvent front travels 8.0 cm. Calculate its \(R_{\text{f}}\) value.
cards.a: \(R_{\text{f}} = 0.45\)
steps: \(R_{\text{f}} = \frac{\text{distance moved by spot}}{\text{distance moved by solvent front}}\)
cards.why: Measure both distances from the start line, to the centre of the spot.

cards.q: In one solvent the \(R_{\text{f}}\) values are: glycine 0.26, alanine 0.38, valine 0.60. An unknown spot moves 4.5 cm and the solvent front 7.5 cm. Identify the amino acid.
cards.a: Valine
steps: This matches the value for valine in the same solvent.
cards.why: \(R_{\text{f}}\) values depend on the solvent and plate, so compare only with values found under the same conditions.

cards.q: Explain why different amino acids travel different distances on a TLC plate.
cards.a: They have different relative affinities for the stationary and mobile phases.
marks: Each amino acid has a different side chain (R group).
So each has a different balance between adsorption to the stationary phase and solubility in the mobile phase.
One held more strongly by the stationary phase moves more slowly and has a lower Rf value.

cards.q: What is the primary structure of a protein?
cards.a: The sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain.
cards.why: It is held by covalent peptide links; it determines how the chain folds.

cards.q: Describe the secondary structure of a protein and how it is maintained.
cards.a: The chain coils into an α-helix or folds into a β-pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds between peptide links.

answerFigure.alt: Hydrogen bond between two sections of protein chain: the δ+ hydrogen of an N–H group in the upper chain is attracted to a lone pair on the δ− oxygen of a C=O group in the lower chain, shown as a dashed line.

cards.why: Hydrogen bonds form between the \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) oxygen of one peptide link and the \(\mathrm{N{-}H}\) hydrogen of another.

cards.q: Explain how hydrogen bonds form between peptide links in a protein.
cards.a: Between a δ+ H on N and a lone pair on a δ− O.

figure.alt: Hydrogen bond between two sections of protein chain: the δ+ hydrogen of an N–H group in the upper chain is attracted to a lone pair on the δ− oxygen of a C=O group in the lower chain, shown as a dashed line.

marks: Nitrogen and oxygen are much more electronegative than hydrogen and carbon.
So the N–H hydrogen is δ+ and the C=O oxygen is δ−.
The δ+ hydrogen is attracted to a lone pair on the δ− oxygen of another peptide link.

cards.q: What is the tertiary structure of a protein, and what holds it in place?
cards.a: The overall 3D folding of the whole chain, held by interactions between R groups: hydrogen bonds, ionic attractions and sulfur–sulfur (disulfide) bonds.
cards.why: Weaker van der Waals forces between non-polar side chains also contribute.

cards.q: How do two cysteine residues form a sulfur–sulfur bond?
cards.a: The \(\mathrm{-SH}\) groups of two cysteines are oxidised, losing two H atoms and forming a covalent \(\mathrm{-S{-}S-}\) bond (disulfide bridge).

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of cysteine: 2-amino-3-sulfanylpropanoic acid, with a CH2SH side chain.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of cystine: two cysteine units joined through their side chains by an S–S bond.

cards.why: The S–S bond is covalent and strong: it locks parts of the chain together, even far apart in the sequence.

cards.q: Explain why heating a protein, or changing its pH, can stop it working.
cards.a: The bonds holding its 3D shape are broken, so the shape changes (it is denatured).
marks: Heat provides energy to break hydrogen bonds.
A change of pH changes the charges on R groups such as –NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻, disrupting ionic attractions and hydrogen bonds.
The tertiary structure changes, so an enzyme’s active site loses its shape.

cards.q: A diagram shows a long chain coiled into a regular spiral, with dashed lines joining every fourth peptide link. Which level of protein structure is this?
cards.a: Secondary structure: an α-helix.
cards.why: The dashed lines are hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups of peptide links four residues apart.

cards.q: What is an enzyme?
cards.a: A protein that acts as a biological catalyst.
cards.why: It provides an alternative reaction route with a lower activation energy.

cards.q: What is the active site of an enzyme?
cards.a: A region of the enzyme, with a specific 3D shape, where the substrate binds and the reaction takes place.
cards.why: Side chains in the active site bind the substrate by hydrogen bonds, ionic attractions and van der Waals forces.

cards.q: Explain why an enzyme’s stereospecific active site binds only one enantiomer of its substrate.
cards.a: Only one enantiomer has its groups arranged in 3D to match the binding points of the active site.
marks: The active site has a specific 3D shape, formed from chiral amino acids.
The substrate must bind at several points, each group to a particular part of the site.
Enantiomers have the same groups in a mirror-image arrangement.
Only one enantiomer can line up all its groups with the binding points at once.

cards.q: How can a drug act as an enzyme inhibitor?
cards.a: Its molecule fits and binds to the active site, blocking it so that the substrate cannot bind.
cards.why: Such a drug has a shape similar to the substrate, so the enzyme’s reaction slows or stops.

cards.q: How are computers used to help design drugs that inhibit enzymes?
cards.a: Computer modelling shows the 3D shape of the active site, so chemists can design and test molecules that fit it before making them.
cards.why: This saves time and money: fewer compounds need to be synthesised and tested in the laboratory.

cards.q: True or false: both enantiomers of a chiral drug always have the same effect in the body because they have the same structural formula.
cards.a: False. Only one enantiomer may fit the target active site or receptor; the other may be inactive or harmful.
cards.why: Thalidomide is the classic example: one enantiomer was a sedative, the other caused birth defects.

cards.q: What is a nucleotide made of?
cards.a: A phosphate group bonded to 2-deoxyribose (a pentose sugar), which is bonded to one of four bases: adenine, cytosine, guanine or thymine.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of a nucleotide, deoxyadenosine monophosphate: a phosphate group bonded to the CH2 of 2-deoxyribose, whose ring carbon is bonded to the base adenine.

cards.why: The structures of the phosphate ion, 2-deoxyribose and the four bases are in the AQA data booklet.

cards.q: Why is the sugar in DNA called 2-deoxyribose?
cards.a: It is ribose with the OH group on carbon 2 replaced by H: it has one oxygen fewer.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of 2-deoxyribose in its five-membered ring form: a ring of four carbons and one oxygen, with OH groups and a CH2OH group, and a CH2 with no OH.

cards.why: “Deoxy” means without an oxygen.

cards.q: How are nucleotides joined in a single strand of DNA?
cards.a: By covalent bonds between the phosphate group of one nucleotide and the 2-deoxyribose of the next, forming a sugar–phosphate backbone with the bases attached to the sugars.
cards.why: Each link forms by condensation, eliminating water. DNA is a condensation polymer.

cards.q: Which bases pair in DNA, and how many hydrogen bonds form in each pair?
cards.a:
Adenine–thymine: 2 hydrogen bonds.
Cytosine–guanine: 3 hydrogen bonds.
cards.why: Each base pair has one larger two-ring base and one smaller one-ring base, so the strands stay a constant distance apart.

cards.q: Explain how hydrogen bonding between bases leads to two complementary strands of DNA.
cards.a: Each base can hydrogen bond fully only with its partner, so the sequence of one strand fixes the other.
marks: Bases contain N–H groups (δ+ H) and lone pairs on N and O atoms (δ−).
Hydrogen bonds form between bases on opposite strands.
The positions of these groups mean A lines up with T (2 hydrogen bonds) and C with G (3 hydrogen bonds), and no other pairing fits.
So the base sequence of one strand determines the other: the strands are complementary, and twist into a double helix.

cards.q: One strand of DNA has the base sequence A T G C C A. Give the sequence of the complementary strand.
cards.a: T A C G G T
steps: A pairs with T, and T with A.
G pairs with C, and C with G.
cards.why: Complementary base pairing.

cards.q: Describe the overall structure of DNA.
cards.a: Two complementary strands, each a sugar–phosphate backbone with bases attached, twisted into a double helix and held together by hydrogen bonds between base pairs.
cards.why: The backbones are on the outside; the base pairs are stacked inside.

cards.q: Which DNA base is this?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of guanine: a fused six-membered and five-membered ring system with an NH2 group and a C=O group on the six-membered ring.

cards.a: Guanine
cards.why: Guanine and adenine have two fused rings; guanine has a C=O, adenine does not. Guanine is the base cisplatin bonds to.

cards.q: Identify this DNA base, and the base it pairs with.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of thymine: a six-membered ring containing two N–H groups, with two C=O groups and a methyl group.

cards.a: Thymine; it pairs with adenine.
cards.why: Thymine and cytosine are single-ring bases; thymine has two C=O groups and a methyl group.

cards.q: True or false: the two strands of DNA are held together by covalent bonds between the bases.
cards.a: False. The strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between bases.
cards.why: Covalent bonds join the nucleotides within each strand; the weaker hydrogen bonds let the strands separate for replication.

cards.q: Describe the structure of cisplatin.
cards.a: A square planar platinum(II) complex, \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_{3})_{2}Cl_{2}]}\), with the two ammonia ligands next to each other (cis) and the two chloride ligands next to each other.

answerFigure.alt: Two square planar platinum(II) complexes. Cisplatin: the two NH3 ligands are next to each other on the left and the two Cl ligands next to each other on the right. Transplatin: each NH3 is opposite the other, and each Cl opposite the other.

cards.why: Transplatin has the same formula but the like ligands are opposite each other; it is not an effective drug.

cards.q: Explain how cisplatin prevents DNA replication in cancer cells.
cards.a: It bonds to guanine bases on DNA by ligand replacement, distorting the strand.
marks: In the cell, a chloride ligand on cisplatin is replaced (ligand replacement).
A bond forms between platinum and a nitrogen atom on a guanine base in DNA.
Both chloride ligands are replaced, so platinum bonds to two guanines, often on the same strand.
This distorts the DNA so the strands cannot separate and be copied: the cell cannot divide.

cards.q: Explain why cisplatin has adverse side effects.
cards.a: It also stops replication in healthy cells.
marks: Cisplatin bonds to the DNA of any cell, not only cancer cells.
Healthy cells that divide rapidly, such as hair follicles and blood cells, are most affected.
This causes effects such as hair loss and a weakened immune system; cisplatin can also damage the kidneys.

cards.q: How is the use of a drug such as cisplatin justified, given its harmful side effects?
cards.a: Society must weigh the benefits (it cures or controls some cancers, such as testicular cancer) against the risks, and doses are kept as low as possible.
cards.why: Cisplatin is given in small doses, in short courses, and directly to the tumour where possible, so healthy cells recover.

cards.q: In the reaction of cisplatin with DNA, what acts as the ligand and what type of bond forms?
cards.a: A nitrogen atom on guanine acts as the ligand: it donates its lone pair to platinum, forming a coordinate (dative covalent) bond.
cards.why: It replaces a chloride ligand: a ligand substitution (replacement) reaction.
